Interest-Rate Risk Factor Swamps Bank Stock Valuations 
We think rates have both risks and catalysts; plus, we give updates 
from the Barclays conference earlier this month. 
Understand How Interest-Rate Movements Will Drive Bank Valuations in Current Environment  
While company-specific results have seemed to matter during earnings, improved valuations for banks 
have had a hard time holding up over time. Why is this? We believe an interest-rate risk factor is 
overriding most idiosyncratic factors for now. The first risk is the potential for higher short-term rates. 
Higher rates are typically good for bank profits. Today, they are not. Further, if rates get high enough, 
more banks could start breaking. The second risk is the potential for higher long-term rates. The higher 
longer-term rates go, the larger the losses become within accumulated other comprehensive income, or 
AOCI, and the longer it takes to satisfy upcoming regulatory capital rules.  
 
We think third-quarter results may be the first quarter since March 8 when we see net interest income, 
or NII, guidance stay stable, and we expect some positive reaction to this. However, we also expect that 
bank valuations will need the market to become more confident that the current rate hike cycle is indeed 
over for an additional rerating higher. Our base case is that all the banks under our coverage will survive 
this rate cycle and eventually meet the new regulatory requirements. Our sense is the market is still not 
entirely convinced, and this likely explains a material portion of the disconnection between our current 
fair value estimates and current valuations. We see the most risk in Comerica, KeyCorp, and Zions on the 
profitability front, and Truist, KeyCorp, and Schwab on the capital front.

Key Takeaways  
× Today, higher interest rates are a negative for the banking sector. Higher short-term rates are a negative 
for profitability because of higher funding costs. Higher long-term rates are a negative for meeting 
upcoming regulatory capital requirements. Rates will be a key determinant of bank valuations for now. 
× Warning: Higher rates also present tail risks. If rates go high enough, more banks could start breaking. If 
more banks start to break, valuations for the whole sector will suffer. 
× Our base case is that all the banks under our coverage will survive this rate cycle and eventually meet 
the new regulatory requirements. Our sense is the market is still not entirely convinced. If rates go 
materially higher from here, our base case could start to unravel for several names. This likely explains a 
material portion of the disconnection between our fair value estimates and current valuations.  
× We see the most risk in Comerica, KeyCorp, and Zions on the profitability front, and Truist, KeyCorp, and 
Schwab on the capital front. 
× While KeyCorp and Zions are riskier with regards to profitability, there are some potential positives. 
KeyCorp's unique NII boost between now and first-quarter 2025 should materially improve the bank's 
positioning. Our impression is that the market does not want to give the bank any upfront credit for this, 
so to the extent that the bank can survive and see a material boost to its NII over the next three to six 
quarters, it could be a positive catalyst. Zions has shown some surprising resilience within its NII over 
the past two months, with NII bottoming in June and growing in July and August. This suggests 
earnings pressure may not be as bad going forward as what we saw in second-quarter results. 
× KeyCorp presents the highest risk for a dividend cut among our coverage, with a dividend payout ratio 
that is likely to expand into the 80% range, even without additional rate hikes. If the Federal Reserve 
hikes again, it could start to push the payout ratio above 100%, increasing the odds of a dividend cut. By 
the first quarter of 2024, we estimate the improvement in the bank's NII should buy it an ability to 
absorb one more additional rate hike before its payout ratio breaches 100%. No additional rate hikes 
would be the best scenario for the bank. 
× Maintaining current rates for longer ("higher for longer," without going higher than today) is not a bad 
scenario for the banks. Eventually securities yields will improve, providing an earnings boost over time. 
We think the key for bank valuations will be about the "higher" and not the "longer." 
× The most recent updates we have from the banks came during the Barclays conference, which ran from 
Sept. 11 through 13. We viewed the latest updates as largely positive. A few banks (Huntington, 
Comerica, and M&T) were seeing some increased expense pressure, but NII outlooks were maintained 
(U.S. Bancorp was the only bank admitting to some extra pressure).  
× The latest regulatory impact estimates from the Barclays conference also largely aligned with our own 
internal estimates, with risk-weighted assets, or RWAs, expected to grow midsingle digits for most 
regionals, while larger banks are set to grow 20% or more. Morgan Stanley and Citigroup both surprised 
us positively with lower RWA growth estimates than we expected. We estimate the impact of additional 
long-term debt issuance would be a low-single-digit percentage of earnings. 
× Top Picks: Wells Fargo, PNC, and M&T. We see all three names as cheap, but without the rate risk of the 
cheapest names, presenting a more attractive risk/reward profile for investors looking to avoid the 
biggest risks. However, all banks will have some correlation with rate movements and therefore some

What Is Driving Bank Valuations Lately? Banks Cannot Seem to Hold On to Postearnings Gains  
Heading into first-quarter earnings, which were our first look at bank results since the collapse of Silicon 
Valley on March 10 and the resulting banking industry pressure, our thesis was that the market would 
reward banks that avoided a bank run, while further punishing banks that were falling apart. Instead, 
the market yawned, with the banking sector largely treading water despite most banks under our 
coverage seeing only a low-single-digit percentage decline in their deposit bases. Our read on this, after 
the fact, was that the market was in "wait-and-see" mode and was not convinced that the turmoil was 
truly over after first-quarter results. In other words, "today's results aren't terrible, but we're still very 
worried about tomorrow's results."

What Is Driving Bank Valuations Lately? A Key Factor Is Interest-Rate Risk 
While banks may be proving to the market in the past several quarters that their deposit bases are not 
disappearing and they are remaining relatively profitable, interest-rate movements still seem to be the 
main factor driving valuations, for now. 
 
Higher Short-Term Rates Are Negative Catalyst 
Higher rates are typically good for bank profits. Today, higher rates are bad for profitability due to higher 
funding costs. Further, if rates get high enough, more banks could start breaking. While the banks that 
survived have proven they are categorically different than the banks that failed, if the Federal Reserve 
hikes rates high enough, those categories could get blurry again. For some banks, this potential breaking 
point seems closer than for others.  
 
Higher Long-Term Rates Are Negative Catalyst 
Higher long-term interest rates are also not great for banks in the current environment. Typically, banks 
would want to see an upward sloping yield curve. If that occurred today, the 10-year treasury yield 
would need to increase over 100 basis points. This has the potential to materially increase the unrealized 
losses on securities on bank balance sheets and therefore delay how long it takes Category III and IV 
banks to satisfy upcoming regulatory capital requirements. This makes higher long-term interest rates 
another risk investors are likely wary about. 
 
We think it is this mix of factors that is linking bank valuations with short term rate expectations and 
long-term rates. As a result, rate movements are largely overrunning any idiosyncratic factors, becoming 
one of the only factors that currently matters for bank valuations.

Interest-Rate Risk Is Real: Higher Short-Term Rates Drive up Funding Costs, Reduce Profitability 
Profitability outlooks have fallen for most banks following March 8 as competition for deposits has 
heated up and funding costs have soared. A common way to measure deposit costs is deposit betas, 
defined as the change in the cost of interest-bearing deposits divided by the change in the federal-funds 
rate. Intuitively, if the Federal Reserve hikes rates 100 basis points and a bank's interest-bearing deposit 
costs increase 100 basis points, that is a beta of 100%. Betas have soared following March 8. While it is 
typical for betas to rise in the late stages of an interest-rate cycle, betas this cycle have been a bit higher 
than the most recent 2015-19 cycle and are inching closer to what we saw during pre-2015 cycles. This 
has been a shock to the system, as betas were trending closer to the 2015 cycle before March 8, and 
since then betas have accelerated faster than previously expected.

each quarter, removing the effects of balance sheet growth, and comparing that to how much interest

net income. The intuition is "this is how much each additional rate hike will decrease earnings."

Most banks we cover are negatively exposed to rates in the current environment, particularly among 
regional banks and Schwab. KeyCorp, Comerica, and Zions are under the most pressure and we believe 
they have the highest interest-rate profitability risk within their businesses today. If the Federal Reserve 
were to push rates materially higher, to 6.25% or 6.5%, these would likely be the first banks under our 
coverage to start to really get hurt. Under these more dire scenarios, we would likely see dividend cuts 
and increases in the tail risk of going unprofitable and seeing additional deposit flight as the depositors 
reassessed the viability of these banks.  
 
The recent decrease in Charles Schwab's NII is more from clients reallocating assets from low-cost 
sweep cash deposits into higher cost certificates of deposits and money market funds. The rate paid on 
the company's sweep cash deposits has remained low at 0.45% (as of Sept. 21, 2023), but overall 
funding costs have increased from the company having to utilize supplemental funding, such as CDs and 
Federal Home Loan Bank loans, to replace the sweep deposits. For our analysis and thoughts on the 
liquidity, capital, and deposit-movement issues that have depressed Charles Schwab’s share price in 
2023, please see our August report, Finding Comfort With Charles Schwab’s Uncertainties. 
 
Our base case, and indeed the market's base case, is that the federal-funds rate has already peaked and 
there will be no more hikes, so three to four additional hikes from here do not seem likely. However, 
investors a year ago would have thought a federal-funds rate of 5.25% today looked almost impossible, 
so it is an important risk to keep in mind. These would be the three banks to potentially "break" first 
under a tail risk type of interest-rate environment. We think this is a risk driving valuations for the banks 
under our coverage, especially for the banks more exposed to these risks, and investors should keep this 
in mind. 
 
Zions and KeyCorp Have Some Nuanced Resistance to the Rate Pressure Narrative 
KeyCorp has a unique potential boost coming to its NII from now until first-quarter 2025. The bank 
previously put on hedges that in retrospect were not ideal. As these money losing swaps expire and as 
lower rate treasures expire, management expects a roughly $900 million annualized, or $230 million 
quarterly boost to NII. This is equivalent to a 24% increase in the bank's most recent quarterly NII. This is 
material and unique. We do not believe any other bank under our coverage is being hurt by their 
hedging and securities books as much as KeyCorp. If KeyCorp can get this entire benefit, it would buy 
the bank an extra buffer of roughly three additional rate hikes by our estimates. If the bank's unique NII 
boost story does play out, the bank should be a bit safer than it currently looks. Our impression is that 
the market does not want to give the bank any upfront credit for this, so to the extent that the bank can 
"prove it" and have some material boosts to its NII over the next three to six quarters, we think it could 
prove positive for the bank's current valuation as it is both idiosyncratic and helps deal with some of the 
rate risk narrative.

This situation also introduces some timing risk. If the Fed hikes rates sooner rather than later, KeyCorp 
will not have had as much time to improve its NII situation. The market currently thinks it is a coin toss 
between a "no more hikes" or "at least one more hike" for the December, January, and March Federal 
Reserve meetings. KeyCorp presents the highest risk for a dividend cut among our coverage, with a 
dividend payout ratio that is likely to expand into the 80% range, even without any more rate hikes. If 
the Federal Reserve hikes even one more time, it could start to push the payout ratio above 100%, 
increasing the odds of a dividend cut. By the first quarter of 2024, we estimate the theoretical 
improvement in the bank's NII positioning should buy it the ability to absorb one more rate hike before 
the payout ratio exceeds 100%. So, if the Fed hikes rates in December, it will be worse for the bank than

Interest-Rate Risk Is Real: Higher Longer-Term Interest Rates Increase Unrealized Losses 
While higher short-term rates are currently a net negative for the banking sector, higher longer-term 
rates are also not helping either. Most banks have unrealized losses on securities on their balance 
sheets due to rates moving higher over the past year and a half. Unrealized losses on available for sale 
securities flow into accumulated other comprehensive income, or AOCI, and this affects capital ratios for 
Category I and II banks (the largest banks) and will eventually affect capital ratios for the smaller banks 
that are still larger than $100 billion in assets (Category III and IV).  
 
New regulations will start phasing in on July 1, 2025. Today, smaller banks do not currently have to 
include AOCI in their regulatory capital ratios. If they were forced to include AOCI and therefore include 
the unrealized losses, they would not always be meeting regulatory capital minimums. This sets up a 
race to meet changing capital requirements. One key lever in this race is the level of unrealized losses 
within AOCI. The higher longer-term rates go, the larger the losses become within AOCI, and the longer 
it takes to amortize away these discounts and satisfy the upcoming regulatory capital rules.

Research Methodology for Valuing Companies 
 
Overview 
At the heart of our valuation system is a detailed projection of a company's future cash flows, resulting from our analysts' research. 
Analysts create custom industry and company assumptions to feed income statement, balance sheet, and capital investment 
assumptions into our globally standardized, proprietary discounted cash flow, or DCF, modeling templates. We use scenario 
analysis, in-depth competitive advantage analysis, and a variety of other analytical tools to augment this process. We think 
analyzing valuation through discounted cash flows presents a better lens for viewing cyclical companies, high-growth firms, 
businesses with finite lives (mines, for example), or companies expected to generate negative earnings over the next few years. 
That said, we don't dismiss multiples altogether but rather use them as supporting cross-checks for our DCF-based fair value 
estimates. We also acknowledge that DCF models offer their own challenges (including a potential proliferation of estimated 
inputs and the possibility that the method may miss short-term market-price movements), but we believe these negatives are 
mitigated by deep analysis and our long-term approach.  
 
Morningstar's Equity Research Group ("we," "our") believes that a company's intrinsic worth results from the future cash flows it 
can generate. The Morningstar Rating for stocks identifies stocks trading at a discount or premium to their intrinsic worth—or fair 
value estimate in Morningstar terminology. Five-star stocks sell for the biggest risk-adjusted discount to their fair values, whereas 
1-star stocks trade at premiums to their intrinsic worth.  
 
Four key components drive the Morningstar rating:  
× our assessment of the firm's economic moat.  
× our estimate of the stock's fair value.  
× our uncertainty around that fair value estimate.  
× the current market price.  
 
This process ultimately culminates in our single-point star rating.  
 
Economic Moat 
The Morningstar Economic Moat Rating is a structural feature that Morningstar believes positions a firm to earn durable excess 
profits over a long period of time, with excess profits defined as returns on invested capital above our estimate of a firm’s cost of 
capital. The economic moat rating is not an indicator of the investment performance of the investment highlighted in this report. 
Narrow-moat companies are those that Morningstar believes are more likely than not to achieve normalized excess returns for at 
least the next 10 years. Wide-moat companies are those that Morningstar believes will earn excess returns for 10 years, with 
excess returns more likely than not to remain for at least 20 years. Firms without a moat, including those that have a substantial 
threat of value destruction-related risks related to environmental, social, and governance; industry disruption; financial health; or 
other idiosyncratic issues, are more susceptible to competition. Morningstar has identified five sources of economic moats: 
intangible assets, switching costs, network effect, cost advantage, and efficient scale. 
 
Fair Value Estimate 
Each stock's fair value is estimated by using a proprietary discounted cash flow model, which assumes that the stock's value is 
equal to the total of the free cash flows of the company is expected to generate in the future, discounted back to the present at 
the rate commensurate with the riskiness of the cash flows. As with any DCF model, the ending value is highly sensitive to
